data.title: BankThink Blocking AI agents is the right near-term move for banks
data.description:
• Key insight: The industry won't be able to fend off customers' use of outside AI agents forever. Right now, though, bankers have an opportunity to begin creating the policies and procedures that will govern them in the future.
  • Forward look: With good reasons to move slowly, banks should seize this opportunity to address long-standing weaknesses while preparing for a new way of doing business.

Jamie Dimon has long been an enthusiastic advocate for technology. He's made AI a strategic priority at JPMorganChase and backed a $19.8 billion technology budget for 2026. So, when the CEO of America's largest bank says outside AI agents are too risky to allow into customer accounts, we should take note.

Morgan Stanley, Bank of America and Citi are also restricting third-party agents, and for good reason. Axios reports that banks are already detecting agents accessing customer accounts, sometimes taking actions beyond what customers authorized.

The liability concerns are justified. Right now, there is little consensus on who's responsible when an agent transfers money without permission. Is it the bank, the customer or the company that built the agent? Most online banking agreements were written with human customers in mind, not autonomous software acting on their behalf.

Even though some banks have already rewritten their terms of service to address these questions (usually assigning liability to the customer that authorized the agent to act on their behalf), changing the fine print won't necessarily settle them. And we've seen how quickly assumptions about liability can change.

With authorized push payment, or APP,  scams, victims are tricked into approving payments to fraudsters. Since the customer authorized the transaction, it was defensible that they were liable for the losses. But as losses mounted, regulators stepped in. In the U.K., banks are now required to reimburse victims in most qualifying cases, even if they authorized the payments. If AI agents start making costly mistakes, banks shouldn't assume today's liability rules will be the final word.

Not to mention, banks have spent decades building customer relationships and don't want to cede that ground to third-party software. On the one hand, banks and fintechs want their product offers to be discoverable by agents, and on the other, those same agents could make it much easier for consumers to shop for better rates and move money between institutions, threatening the loyalty and deposit relationships banks depend on.

How, then, can banks let third-party agents in safely?

Charles Schwab is blocking unauthorized agents while developing controlled ways for customers to connect AI assistants to their accounts (and pushing the use of its consumer-facing agent, Charley).

Meanwhile, six banks, including Bank of America and Capital One, have published principles for establishing trust in agentic commerce. They emphasize transparency, consumer consent, fraud protection and freedom to choose agent services.

Read more:

  • Why some community banks are going slow on AI adoption
  • How an alleged fake-CEO scheme took $2.7 million from R.I. bank
  • JPMorganChase to use OpenAI models for coding, security
  • OCC: Banks need strong controls when delegating to AI agents

Both approaches recognize that banks need safeguards beyond a blanket prohibition. But approved connections don't eliminate fraud risk. They can actually introduce risks that existing safeguards weren't designed to catch.

Take the case of a criminal operating dozens of mule accounts. An agent that can't transfer money could still monitor balances across those accounts. Banks might ordinarily detect suspicious patterns when someone accesses multiple unrelated accounts. But when those requests come through an approved AI connection, some familiar warning signs may be absent.

Blocking agents at login presents another problem. FFIEC's guidance calls for risk-based authentication, but AI agents complicate matters. A customer can log in legitimately and then hand control to an agent, which may act in ways the customer never intended. So, knowing who logged in is no longer enough; banks need to know what's happening the whole time they're inside. It's an open question if the FFIEC's original guidance will be updated to require agent-specific controls.

Furthermore, the technology is changing faster than the industry can keep up, and the infrastructure needed to secure and govern agentic systems is still evolving. While banks have spent years dealing with account takeovers, unauthorized transactions and fraud committed using legitimate credentials, the speed, scale and independence with which agents can operate is new. The banks' position paper acknowledges their five principles must be backed by technical controls not yet in place.

So, this is no place for a "move fast and break things" approach.

This isn't solely a technology problem, either. Modern security and fraud infrastructure needs to enable fraud, cybersecurity and compliance teams to better share information and understand how agent activity could affect their respective responsibilities. If they remain siloed, each may see part of a suspicious interaction without recognizing the broader risk.

But there is an opportunity here. The tightened controls needed for AI agents can improve detection of "traditional" scams and fraud, provided fraud and security systems treat human and agent interactions holistically. Customers would benefit from stronger safeguards and greater freedom to use new financial services, with fraud and security teams being able to react more dynamically to a changing threat landscape.

With good reasons to move slowly, banks should seize this opportunity to address long-standing weaknesses while preparing for a new way of doing business.

Let's use this time wisely.

data.title: Bank stablecoins are about to flood the market. Are there too many?
data.description:
• Key insight: Banks have invested $270 million in Project Faro
  • Forward look: The next period is proving scalability and economic viability, according to Celent's Alenka Grealish.

Project Faro's bank-led stablecoin venture this week took a big step forward with a $270 million five-year funding commitment.
If the news sounds familiar it's probably because it is. Faro is one of several stablecoin ventures in various stages of development as banks consider how to adopt emerging digital assets that are still not widely used for payments or to perform other financial services. 

Payment experts say the growing roster of group efforts are creating healthy competition, at least for now. "The short answer is no, there aren't too many stablecoin groups, but with a qualifier that it's over the next two years," Alenka Grealish, a senior research and advisory leader at Celent, told American Banker. "Beyond that, yes there are too many stablecoin groups."

Bank stablecoins

There are 21 banks in Project Faro, including Goldman Sachs, Citi, Banco Santander and Deutsche Bank. These banks have committed $270 million to fund the project over the next five years, according to Bloomberg.  The four banks mentioned did not return a request for comment. 

The project plans to launch a stablecoin in the first half of 2027, according to a September announcement, with other stablecoins linked to other currencies, including the Euro, in the future. Wells Fargo, Fidelity, UBS and Lloyds have also been tied to the effort. Faro is working on its stablecoin as at least one bank stablecoin consortium has gone live. Open Standard's OUSD stablecoin launched in October, bringing together more than 140 banks, fintechs, payment companies and crypto firms. Its stablecoin has attracted BNY, U.S. Bank, Huntington Bank, Citizens Bank, Cross River, The Bancorp and Pathward. 

HSBC in late October launched RedCoin, a stablecoin in Hong Kong through HSBC's PayMe P2P network, covering about 3.3 million users. RedCoin is regulated by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority and backed by Hong Kong dollars.

"We're in the Cambrian period of market development with stablecoins demonstrating value and feasibility and thereby driving investment," Grealish said. "Heated competition pushes the art of the possible."

Getting ready

There is growing bank interest in stablecoins. Cross-border payment fintech Payoneer surveyed 265 senior payments, treasury and finance leaders at U.S.-based e-commerce marketplaces, platforms and enterprises with $100 million or more in annual revenue, reporting 97% are using, testing or still evaluating stablecoins. Within that group, 69% are actively supporting stablecoins in real operations.

The next period is proving scalability and economic viability, according to Grealish. "Few stablecoin initiatives will survive," she said. "The current market structure is already highly concentrated in Circle and Tether. The scaling winners will be those that support real world economy flows, abstract the blockchain, deliver a friendly user experience and provide battle tested cybersecurity and resiliency."

Tokenized deposits, a lower-risk, more closed alternative to stablecoins, are a bit more popular among banks, but tokenized deposits are not taking the place of stablecoin strategies.

Twenty-four of the largest 50 banks have tokenized deposits "on their radar" as of the first quarter, up from 19 the prior quarter, according to American Banker research on digital assets. That compares to the 17 banks that have stablecoins on their radar, up from 15 in the fourth quarter of 2025.

"Having multiple, substantially interoperable stablecoin consortiums and individual issuers competing in the market is healthy," Eric Grover, a principal at Intrepid Ventures, told American Banker, adding that these models—each with different governance, participants, approaches to distribution, yield-sharing, target markets and incentives for use—are vying for share. "Their models will evolve based on market traction. Competition, with iterative enhancements driven by market feedback, will make most of them better."The banks are competing with fintechs such as Tether and Circle, which have had stablecoins in the market for several years.

Read more:

  • Bankers swing to negative view on funding costs: Survey
  • How agentic commerce is changing the customer experience
  • Why the FTC and 8 states are suing payments fintech Toast
  • $6B Binance heist provokes stablecoin freeze dilemma

"A single issuer like Tether has the advantage of capturing all the economics and maintaining greater control, which gives it speed and agility in the market," Grover said.
In contrast, a consortium like Open USD will inevitably move slower, but aims to achieve greater network critical mass by leveraging its 140-plus participants and sharing the lion's share of its economics with its participants that route, adopt, and distribute its stablecoins, according to Grover.

"While the analogs aren't perfect, in the 19th century, thousands of banks issued banknotes that interoperated through clearinghouses," Grover said. "Today, we have multiple—but not thousands of—competing electronic payment networks. There won't be a single winner, and some of the models recently announced or already launched will fail."

data.title: How banks can prepare for Democrats' oversight era
data.description:
• Key insight: Affordability arguments have been some of banks' most successful lobbying messages over the last two years, and may be their best defense against Democratic inquiries in the next Congress. 
  • Forward look: Connections with notorious sex trafficker Jeffrey Epstein, cryptocurrency entanglements and data privacy concerns at the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau are the most likely topics for congressional inquiry, experts say. 

WASHINGTON — As a new crop of lawmakers begin to arrive on Capitol Hill, committee gavels and members are fleshing out their platforms for the next two years. 

For Democrats, who will control both the House and Senate in the 120th Congress, oversight of the Trump administration and the industries that have profited from its policies will be a central plank of their governing platform. Sen. Ron Wyden, chair of the Senate Finance Committee, has said he will target Wall Street banks that had a relationship with disgraced financier Jeffrey Epstein, and experts anticipate that crypto companies, especially those tied to the administration, will also receive heightened attention. 

In the Senate Banking Committee — which is expected to be led by Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., a key architect of the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau — the Trump administration's dismantling of that agency and the financial data that Elon Musk and the so-called Department of Government Efficiency could have accessed will be center stage. 

For bankers, this means a heightened risk of being caught in an unflattering spotlight or on the periphery of congressional investigations — a potentially pricey and time-consuming prospect, not unlike the negative attention the industry faced in the wake of the 2008 financial crisis.

But banks have a different playbook this time than they had in that post-crisis era — many have spent the last few years convincing lawmakers that they have a valuable role to play in solving the affordability crisis and in safely lending to Main Streets across the country. Stephen Gannon, a partner at Davis Wright Tremaine, said that might be banks' best defense going forward. 

"I think banks come into this round of oversight with an advantage, which is they've had years now of building up capital and liquidity," Gannon said. "So they've got very strong balance sheets, very strong profitability, very good records of investing in their communities, and there's no major product out there that has people worked up." 

Large banks in particular are always adept at communicating with lawmakers in Washington, Gannon said, and should already be prepping strategies to account for the incoming Democratic majority. 

"They've already thought about this, my guess is, with some depth," he said. "The way I'd be preparing is reminding myself of what I've already done, and then gathering data and preparing to tell the story in a way that [positively accentuates] management choices that have been made." 

Jason Abel, a partner at law firm Steptoe LLP, said that one way banks can get ahead of the coming Democratic scrutiny is by highlighting their efforts to improve affordability for American households. Making banks part of the solution rather than part of the problem in lawmakers' eyes will be decisive, he said. 

"I would even say that when it comes to oversight, there is going to be a mention not just on accountability, but tying those issues back into affordability issues and really kitchen table issues as well," Abel said. 

Read more:

  • OCC: Banks need strong controls when delegating to AI agents
  • Democratic wave gives state AGs more enforcement sway
  • Midterm drubbing may complicate GOP lame duck priorities
  • FDIC taking more piecemeal approach to bank failures

Now is a good time, Abel added, "to take stock and understand who your defenders are and who your champions are." 

"We've heard that Democratic counsel are taking notes," he said. "They want to know who responded over the last couple of years to letters that were sent when there were no … gavels in their hands, because the next thing that could arrive could be a subpoena." 

Organizations should be reviewing their prior enforcement actions, any dismissed cases or approved charters that could be the starting point for an investigation. 

"I think that companies and organizations right now can do that [introspection] and start to have a real review internally — and potentially with counsel — about who participated in the discussions around those resolutions," said Ashley Joyner Chavous, a partner at Holland & Knight specializing in congressional investigations. "If there are any particularly interesting or problematic communications around those resolutions, [those should be resolved], and just making sure the stated rationale for those outcomes matches that contemporaneous record." 

The immediate task, she said, is identifying where the company's narrative needs explanation and how congressional disclosures could affect outside litigation or parallel regulatory issues. 

"Institutions should also do the work to organize internally to make sure that documents that may be sought can be accessed," she said, adding that banks and other financial firms should know their weaknesses and have a plan to respond — ideally "before the company gets a letter."

data.title: IT software vendor banks use hit with third security threat
data.description:
• What's at stake: Anyone who takes over an IT provider's N-central console inherits control of every client machine on it, including those at banks and credit unions.
  • Forward look: N-central's built-in remote-control feature is unavailable and will be re-enabled in a future fix, according to N-able's release notes.

Overview bullets generated by AI with editorial review.

Late Sunday, a security researcher published code to exploit 33 unpatched flaws in a product many small banks' IT providers use to manage and access bank systems.

N-able, the company that owns and operates N-central, the product, took the hosted version of the product offline shortly after the vulnerabilities became public. By Tuesday night, it had shipped a fix and upgraded all of the servers it runs for customers.

N-central is software that IT providers use to monitor, patch and remotely control their clients' computers. Community banks and credit unions commonly hire such providers, known as managed service providers, or MSPs, to run their IT.

When an IT provider's N-central console (the dashboard it uses to manage client machines) goes dark, the provider loses its view of every client machine it manages. Anyone who takes over that console inherits the same control.

The New York State Department of Financial Services, or NYDFS, told the firms it regulates in an August letter to find out whether any provider supporting their systems runs N-central.

The letter portended trouble; American Banker reported Wednesday that a ransomware group had apparently exploited the very vulnerability about which NYDFS had warned.

So far, the group has claimed six victims, two of which have confirmed a data breach. One of those two is Sawyer Savings Bank, which American Banker identified in August as a potential victim of the initial N-central vulnerability.

More than 500,000 organizations use N-able's software, according to the company's most recent annual report. The report does not say how many use N-central.

The researcher who published the 33 vulnerabilities, Sean Bales, published the code and descriptions of the flaws on GitHub late Sunday, calling the collection Able2Shell.

N-able took the hosted version of N-central offline in the Americas, Europe and Asia-Pacific on Monday and told customers that run N-central on their own servers to take those servers offline, according to its status page.

The company released the fix at 3:48 p.m. Eastern time Tuesday. At 8:04 p.m., it said on the status page that all hosted servers "across all global regions have been successfully upgraded."

Hosted environments "are back online," an N-able spokesperson told American Banker on Wednesday.

N-able is "observing scanning activity associated with the published proof-of-concept code," according to N-able's status page. In other words, someone (potentially an attacker) is searching the internet for servers against which Bales' exploit code could work.

Huntress, a security firm that monitors MSPs' systems and calls them its partners, "has not observed evidence of Able2Shell exploitation in our partners' environments," according to a Tuesday evening update to its blog post on the flaws.

What the fix leaves for IT providers

The fix addresses "the most critical November 9 vulnerabilities," and "a follow-up hotfix will be released to provide further security updates," N-able said on the status page.

A bank can't install the fix itself. Providers that run N-central on their own servers have to install it. Until they do, those servers should "remain offline," according to the status page.

All customers, including those on N-able's hosted service, also have to upgrade the N-central software installed on each machine they manage, according to the fix's release notes.

N-central's built-in remote-control feature "is currently unavailable and will be re-enabled in a future fix," according to the notes.

As such, any bank whose IT provider uses a self-hosted instance of N-central (as opposed to an instance that N-able hosts) must make sure its provider installs the fix.

The third emergency since August

This week's outage is the third security emergency N-central has had since August.

Attackers began exploiting an earlier N-central flaw July 31, and N-able released a fix Aug. 2. The New York department issued its letter Aug. 11 and later said the flaw had affected a "limited number" of the firms it regulates.

A ransomware group Microsoft tracks as Storm-1175 was likely exploiting that August flaw, Microsoft said in an Aug. 7 post.

In September, N-able fixed a flaw that let attackers run code on an N-central server without logging in. The federal government's vulnerability database lists the flaw as known to be exploited and shows N-able's own severity rating for it: 10 out of 10.

When it released that fix, N-able said it had "no confirmations that this vulnerability has been exploited in production environments," according to the release notes.

Three days later, the company said it had "observed a handful of successful exploits against N-central customers," according to an update to its blog.

The researcher who published new vulnerabilities on Sunday

Bales originally posted his research under the GitHub name Oracle-Security, where a disclosure policy said he publishes when vendors "were unresponsive or took too long in previous responsible disclosures." On Wednesday, he renamed the account and deleted the policy.

Public information does not suggest Bales works for or is endorsed by Oracle, a multinational IT company that produces database software and other products. (A spokesperson for Oracle did not immediately respond to a request for comment.)

N-able said in a statement that claims it "ignored responsible disclosure" from Bales are "inaccurate." Publishing exploit code before customers can act "hands attackers a head start," John Pagliuca, N-able's CEO, told American Banker in a statement.

Bales did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

data.title: Wells Fargo whistleblower argues SEC played 'fast and loose'
data.description:
• Key insight: A lawyer for Wells Fargo's former chief security officer argues that the Securities and Exchange Commission had political motives when it reduced a large whistleblower award to his client.
  • Forward look: The SEC's response to the former Wells Fargo executive's appeal of its decision is due on Dec. 21.

The former chief security officer at Wells Fargo is accusing the Securities and Exchange Commission of playing "fast and loose with its own rules" in a court filing that argues the agency's $54.5 million whistleblower award to him is far smaller than the law requires.

Michael Bacon, who helped the federal government uncover widespread sales misconduct at Wells Fargo, contends that he's owed around $300 million, based on whistleblower statutes.

The SEC's whistleblower program has a statutory minimum of 10% of what has been collected. Wells paid roughly $3 billion to the Department of Justice and the SEC in connection with its phony-accounts fiasco.

Bacon agreed to accept an $179.5 million award back in 2024, but that amount was never finalized, and last year the SEC revised its determination down to $54.5 million. Bacon started the appeals process earlier this year.

In a filing Friday with the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit, Bacon's lawyer asked the judges to either order the SEC to grant a 10% award or reinstate the $179.5 million figure.

The public version of the filing contains redactions, and the filing does not refer to Bacon by his real name since the whistleblower process is confidential.

The SEC's decision to make a downward revision to its award determination for Bacon came in May 2025, just two weeks after Paul Atkins, an appointee of President Trump, was sworn in as the agency's chairman.

Bacon's lawyer, Vince McKnight, argued in his filing that the timeline "makes obvious" that the SEC's downward revision was a "political reversal associated with a change in the SEC chair."

"Such agency action 'dictated or pressured by external forces' is contrary to law," McKnight wrote. "The SEC has thus played fast and loose with its own rules when it suits them."

An SEC spokesperson declined to comment. Its written response to Bacon's filing is due on Dec. 21. Oral arguments in the case are expected to be held in 2027.

Before Atkins joined the SEC, he was sharply critical of whistleblower-award programs. The SEC's program offers payments to claimants of between 10% and 30% of the penalties collected through enforcement actions. The goal is to incentivize the uncovering of corporate malfeasance.

In 2011, as Congress was mulling beefing up whistleblower-award programs, Atkins, then a visiting scholar at the conservative American Enterprise Institute, testified that "the unintended consequences of unfounded charges from disgruntled employees with ulterior motives will be devastating for shareholders."

Better Markets, an advocacy group that favors strong whistleblower protections, found that in fiscal year 2025, the SEC awarded the lowest amount to whistleblowers in the last five fiscal years.

"They are looking for hyper-technical reasons to disqualify someone who was qualified, which is the exact opposite of what Congress intended," Stephen Kohn, a whistleblowing advocacy lawyer, told Bloomberg Law last year. "There has been a policy shift to where resources are now being used to figure out ways to avoid paying qualified claims."

Bacon, who left Wells Fargo in 2014, started meeting with U.S. government officials in the fall of 2016, as the bank's unauthorized-accounts scandal was erupting.

He later told American Banker, which published a five-part series on Bacon's experiences, that he was able to demystify the scandal at an early stage of the government's probes. He has laid blame for the scandal — which involved low-level employees desperate to meet sales targets opening customer accounts without their permission — primarily at the feet of several former top Wells Fargo executives.

Read more:

  • OCC: Banks need strong controls when delegating to AI agents
  • Democratic wave gives state AGs more enforcement sway
  • Midterm drubbing may complicate GOP lame duck priorities
  • FDIC taking more piecemeal approach to bank failures

Bacon has previously received some compensation for the information he provided to the government.

He was awarded $1.6 million by the Justice Department — the maximum amount payable to whistleblowers under the Financial Institutions Reform, Recovery and Enforcement Act of 1989 — though he ultimately received substantially less after subtracting attorneys' fees, taxes and other expenses.

McKnight said in an interview that Bacon's case has important implications beyond how much money the former Wells Fargo executive ultimately receives.

"Whistleblowers rely on a certain consistency and certainty in result," he added. "If you take that away, then that discourages whistleblowers."

data.title: Bank of America agrees to settle fake-accounts suit
data.description:
• Key insight: A 2023 lawsuit against Bank of America piggybacked on a finding by the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau that BofA had opened unauthorized accounts as early as 2012.
  • Forward look: Lawyers for the two sides are asking a judge to set a Jan. 11 deadline for the plaintiffs to move for preliminary approval.

After three years, Bank of America has agreed to settle a class-action lawsuit brought by customers who accused the bank of opening accounts without their permission.

Court documents filed Monday show the nation's second-largest bank has reached a "settlement in principle" with the plaintiffs, though the parties still need to hammer out a definitive agreement. The size of the pending settlement was not disclosed.

The lawsuit dates back to July 2023, when a group of BofA customers accused the $3.4 trillion-asset bank of opening credit cards and other products in their name — unbeknownst to them — and then charging for their use.

The suit was filed two days after the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau ordered BofA to pay $250 million in fines and restitution over an assortment of alleged customer abuses, including unauthorized credit card accounts. According to the CFPB, those accounts dated back to at least 2012.

The CFPB stated in 2023 that "in response to sales pressure or to obtain incentive rewards," BofA "employees sometimes submitted applications for and issued credit cards without customers' consent," though the agency noted that the practice "involved a small percentage" of new accounts.

The class-action suit piggybacked on the CFPB's findings.

"Bank of America routinely — and shockingly — opened consumer accounts for products without the consumer's authorization or knowledge," lawyers for the customers wrote in their complaint, filed in North Carolina federal court. "Then, when customers fail to maintain mandatory account balances or pay fees for accounts that they did not know existed, Bank of America charges the consumer penalties and/or other fees."

On Wednesday, BofA declined to comment on the lawsuit or its potential settlement. Lawyers for the plaintiffs did not respond to American Banker's request for comment.

Attorneys for the two sides are asking a judge to set a Jan. 11 deadline for the plaintiffs to move for preliminary approval.

In court filings, lawyers for the customers had claimed BofA opened the accounts in order to boost profits. The bank's business model, they argued in the complaint, was "based in large part on enrolling consumers in as many banking products as possible." They also wrote that "unrealistic sales quotas" pushed the bank's employees to take increasingly desperate measures.

"Bank of America adopted policies that have, unsurprisingly, driven its bankers to engage in widescale, systemic criminal behavior, including forging consumers' signatures on account applications and abusing access to customers' sensitive information, to meet those unreachable goals," the complaint said.

BofA vigorously denied this, and moved to dismiss the case in November 2024. The unwanted accounts, it theorized, had likely been opened not by BofA employees, but rather by outside fraudsters.

"Bank of America has a clear defense to Plaintiffs' underlying theory of liability: third-party identity theft," the bank's lawyers wrote. "With no factual support for their underlying theory that bank employees secretly opened their accounts to meet sales goals, Plaintiffs' complaint is implausible and must be dismissed."

Read more:

  • Bankers swing to negative view on funding costs: Survey
  • How agentic commerce is changing the customer experience
  • Why the FTC and 8 states are suing payments fintech Toast
  • $6B Binance heist provokes stablecoin freeze dilemma

But in September 2025, a judge only partially granted that order, dismissing certain claims in the complaint but allowing others to move forward. In particular, the judge rejected BofA's use of the identity-fraud theory in an effort to end the lawsuit.

"Defendants' premise that Plaintiffs avoided pleading third-party liability presupposes the existence of facts not in the complaint — that third-party identity thieves opened the unauthorized accounts instead of BoA employees," wrote U.S. District Judge Max Cogburn, Jr. of the Western District of North Carolina.

In August 2020, as the CFPB was investigating the bank, American Banker reported on allegations by former BofA employees of "extreme pressure" to sell credit cards.

In 2019, a BofA lawyer acknowledged to the CFPB that the bank had previously found specific instances of what he called "potentially unauthorized credit card accounts," but he added that multiple analyses provided to the CFPB had consistently identified a "vanishingly small" number of such accounts.

The allegations against BofA came in the wake of an unauthorized-accounts scandal at Wells Fargo, which said in 2017 that its employees had opened 3.5 million potentially unauthorized consumer accounts. The story badly damaged the bank's reputation and ultimately resulted in a $3 billion settlement with the Department of Justice and the Securities and Exchange Commission.

data.title: SEC's enforcement actions fall nearly 24% in 2026
data.description:
• Key insight: Securities and Exchange Commission Chair Paul Atkins said the agency's enforcement program should be judged not by the number of actions filed, but by their effectiveness.
  • Expert quote: "The new Democratic majority in Congress will closely scrutinize whether the Atkins SEC is protecting the American people — or working for scammers and Trump's billionaire buddies on Wall Street." — Senate Banking Committee ranking member Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass.

WASHINGTON — The Securities and Exchange Commission's enforcement actions fell nearly 24% in fiscal 2026, drawing criticism from lawmakers and financial reform advocates over the agency's approach to investor protection.

In its annual report, the agency said its enforcement division filed 348 actions, including 235 standalone actions and 113 "follow-on" administrative proceedings. Those proceedings sought to bar or suspend individuals from participating in certain securities market activities based on factors such as criminal convictions or injunctions.

The total was down from 456 enforcement actions in fiscal 2025 and 583 in fiscal 2024.

In a statement, SEC Chair Paul Atkins said the success of the agency's enforcement program should be measured not by the number of actions filed, but by "how effectively it advances the SEC's mission, protects investors, holds wrongdoers accountable, and strengthens confidence in our markets."

"Enforcement actions and financial remedies are important measures of activity, but they are not the only or most telling measures," he said. "Our responsibility is to apply the law fairly and consistently and ensure that our enforcement efforts advance the Commission's mission. I commend the staff for their dedication to an effective, disciplined enforcement program that serves the investing public."

The report also said the agency obtained orders for $1.095 billion in monetary relief and returned nearly $731 million to more than 250,000 harmed investors. The monetary relief total was down from the adjusted $2.7 billion reported in fiscal 2025, which excluded certain judgments and settlements that were satisfied through separate court proceedings. 

The report drew criticism from Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., who said the decline in enforcement actions would be a focus for Democrats in the coming year. She pointed to a nearly 40% drop in actions since fiscal 2024.

"The new Democratic majority in Congress will closely scrutinize whether the Atkins SEC is protecting the American people — or working for scammers and Trump's billionaire buddies on Wall Street," she wrote in a statement Tuesday.

Read more:

  • OCC: Banks need strong controls when delegating to AI agents
  • Democratic wave gives state AGs more enforcement sway
  • Midterm drubbing may complicate GOP lame duck priorities
  • FDIC taking more piecemeal approach to bank failures

Better Markets, a financial reform advocacy organization, also criticized the decline in enforcement actions and monetary relief, arguing that the figures reflect a retreat from investor protection.

Benjamin Schiffrin, director of securities policy at Better Markets, questioned how the agency plans to measure the effectiveness of its enforcement program.

"Chair Atkins says that 'enforcement actions and financial remedies are important measures of activity, but they are not the only or most telling measures.' Yet it is not clear by what metric he thinks SEC enforcement should be measured," Schiffrin wrote in a statement.

The decline in enforcement actions follows reports of restructuring and layoffs at the SEC. In a letter earlier this year to the agency, Warren said the SEC had lost nearly 20% of its staff, including 13% of employees in the division of enforcement at its headquarters and additional staff across its regional offices.

data.title: CFPB submits servicing final rule for review
data.description:
• Key Insight: What may be coming in the CFPB's newly submitted mortgage servicing final rule.
  • What's at Stake: Whether mortgage servicers will face lighter regulations overall or may end up having to fulfill some new requirements in some areas.
    Overview bullets generated by AI with editorial review. 

The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau has finally sent its long-awaited servicing final rule to an arm of President Trump's executive office for review.

Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs records show it has received the final version of the rule originally proposed near the end of the Biden administration, according to Jonathan Kolodziej, partner at Bradley. 

OIRA's records also confirm earlier Law360 reports that the White House is reviewing the rule. CFPB did not respond to an inquiry.

"We still don't know what is in the rule, but we do know that the CFPB is moving forward," Kolodziej said, while noting there is a lot of speculation about what the version that the White House is likely to greenlight could contain.

Among these are servicing directives from President Trump's March executive order, which experts have said could reshape the bureau's role in the market.

Potential changes for loss mit, servicing errors

"The rumor mill suggests that this final rule will not really look like what the proposal was. Now you know the topics are the same, but the approach that they take for the actual rule, as far as what they require servicers to do, is going to be very different," Kolodziej said.

The March executive order's broader array of mortgage directives include a few that call for CFPB, the Department of Housing and Urban Development, the Federal Reserve, National Credit Union Administration, and banking regulators to update servicing rules.

These include "cure-first standards" for "good-faith servicing errors" and "simplifying loss mitigation requirements." The EO also calls for "aligning supervisory expectations to support portfolio mortgages servicing as a core community banking function."

Directives that call for self-correction of errors over formal penalties and streamlining of rules in the context of the Trump administration's deregulation suggests the servicing final rule likely to emerge some time within the next 90 days will involve lighter regulation.

Less regulation in some areas but potentially more in others

Even the 2023 proposal was considered streamlined relative to some servicing rules the CFPB implemented earlier, incorporating feedback from several industry groups, including the Mortgage Bankers Association, Housing Policy Council and American Bankers Association.

The Trump administration may take this a step further.

"I've heard various approaches that people think this administration might take. One of them is probably more deregulatory, deleting some existing provisions that are viewed as being problematic or overly complicating things. That would certainly be consistent," Kolodziej said.

However, there also is some speculation the final rule could include a mix of scaled-back rules in some areas and additional ones in others as officials have reviewed a broad range of feedback on the original proposal.

"I have also heard some suggestions that they may take the current complex system of regulations and replace it with a new complex system of regulations," Kolodziej said. "That's a big question out there."

data.title: Democrats' affordability mandate could revive swipe-fee fight
data.description:
• Key insight: Affordability, the top issue for voters in last week's elections, could carry along new challenges to interchange, credit-card competition measures and state-level consumer protection enforcement.
  • Supporting data: Nine out of ten voters cited affordability as a major factor in their vote. 

Democrats' affordability mandate, following this month's "blue tsunami," could inject new fervor into state-level pushes to curtail interchange fees and the dominance of credit card networks.
For banks, some of the most immediate pressure could come in the form of crackdowns on interchange fees, or swipe fees, that merchants pay to credit card networks when customers pay with plastic. Nine out of ten voters cited the cost of living as a "major" or "crucial" factor in their vote, according to exit polling conducted by NBC News. Merchant trade groups say they believe lawmakers are more open to consumer protection and merchant-side reforms that lower costs for consumers but could eat into banks' profits. 

"The election results this week show people are very eager for getting at issues that make life less affordable, and credit card swipe fees are one of those problems out there that makes life less affordable for Americans," said Doug Kantor, general counsel of the National Association of Convenience Stores and a representative of the Merchant Payments Coalition. "So I expect there will be more consideration in states and in Congress of ways to deal with that."

Democrats won healthy majorities in both congressional chambers last week, but state level gains were equally pronounced according to a report issued by the National Conference of State Legislatures. The party won six new Democratic trifectas in Arizona, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin — where both houses of congress and the statehouse are controlled by the party. Voters also decided to break at least five Republican trifectas in Georgia, Iowa, New Hampshire, Ohio and Texas, with some results ongoing. Five governorships, in Georgia, Iowa, Nevada, Ohio and Texas are also now controlled by Democrats. Voters overall rewarded campaigns that were laser-focused on the cost of living and policymakers intend to be responsive to those concerns, especially as the 2028 election cycle kicks off. 

Critics of interchange fees say payment systems are opaque, making it impossible to know what interchange fees are charged on any given transaction. Federal Reserve researchers have found that, since merchants often do not set different prices based on payment methods, "merchant acceptance of cards could lead to higher retail prices for all consumers,

including those who pay with alternative methods and receive none of the direct benefits

associated with card use."

Banks charge interchange fees — also known as swipe fees — every time a credit card is used, and those fees are justified as necessary to pay for fraud prevention, the cost of processing the transaction and offsetting the costs of credit card rewards. The fees are set by the card networks such as Visa or Mastercard and often are around 2% to 3% of a transaction. Merchants paid nearly $200 billion in such fees last year. Those costs are often passed on to consumers.

Kantor said he expects swipe fee proposals to surface in more than a dozen states and that lawmakers could consider a variety of methods for cracking down on them through legislation. A model pre-dating the election is the Illinois Interchange Fee Prohibition Act, signed into law by Governor J.B. Pritzker in 2024, which would bar banks and their affiliated card networks from levying such fees on the state sales tax and gratuity portions of transactions, with state officials saying merchants should not be charged for processing non-revenue. 

Getting an anti-swipe fee-measure across the finish line isn't a given though, even in a blue state. Illinois' law is currently on pause following an injunction. Colorado's Democratic legislature also passed a bill to block swipe fees on tax-and-tip-portions of charges, but Democratic Governor Jared Polis vetoed it in June. 

Some states remain mixed politically and will have less authority to move without rigorous debate. Texas, for example, has a new governor in Democrat Gina Hinojosa that has made populist affordability issues a central issue. Last week, in an interview she argued that despite being in Texas, there is room for tackling corporate dominance over average Americans. 

"We have always been a pro-business state in Texas, but what changes now with me as governor is it has to be a partnership that benefits Texans," Hinojosa said in an interview with CNN last week, discussing the need for stronger protections around data centers. "We can have a strong economy, strong industry, and protections for the people of Texas. Those things are not mutually exclusive."

Some, like Chris Furlow, president and CEO of the Texas Bankers Association, argued that banking industry interests will work with policymakers of either party. 

"Whether our elected leaders wear blue or red jerseys, Texans want to build strong futures for their families and businesses, and our priorities haven't changed," Furlow said, adding the group will continue working with lawmakers to fight fraud, promote local lending and ensure regulation is appropriately tailored. "As the eighth largest economy in the world, Texas is now home to more financial services jobs, commercial banks and community banks than any other state. That momentum will continue because policymakers understand that a strong financial sector creates jobs, supports small businesses and keeps our communities growing."

Another issue: what critics say is an anticompetitive credit card network system could also face scrutiny, according to merchant advocates. The Credit Card Competition Act, which has been introduced repeatedly in Congress, would require banks to enable charges over an unaffiliated card network. Kantor says these kinds of measures could also be roped into the affordability agenda. 

"There are some other approaches as well that get at things more like the federal legislation that's out there that says, hey, look, you should at least have competition among the credit card networks," Kantor said. "There may be some of all of those things, and more."

Consumer advocates such as Dennis Kelleher, president of Better Markets, say state attorneys general have, and will continue to, take a more active role in consumer financial protection overall, especially regarding kitchen table issues. 

"These are not merely consumer financial protection issues but also cost of living and affordability issues that certain financial companies make more difficult," Kelleher said. "State lawmakers and agencies will likely continue to address high-cost products offered by fintech companies that target vulnerable consumers, including earned wage access, buy-now-pay-later loans, and merchant cash advances for small businesses."

"One can expect synergy between state attorney generals, consumer groups, and plaintiffs' lawyers to address widespread harms inflicted on financial consumers victimized by financial predators and scammers who are benefiting from if not being incentivized by Trump's CFPB's abandonment of its vital mission and mandate," Kelleher concluded.

data.title: BankThink US payments companies continue to be shut out of China
data.description:
• Key insight: The Chinese government's decades of resistance to allowing U.S. payments networks to compete in China have created an effectively closed market. Recent overtures to Visa don't change that.
  • Forward look: The People's Republic of China's 25-year stall has made a mockery of its WTO commitment. Washington and Visa have no reason to take its latest gesture seriously.

Visa recently received approval from the People's Bank of China, or PBOC, to "begin formal preparations to establish a domestic bankcard clearing institution." Visa hailed it as "a milestone." Credulous media and analysts reported this as progress. It's a milestone on the road to nowhere.

Mainland China's payments market remains de facto closed.

For a quarter of a century, Visa and China have pretended that the world's largest retail payment network had a real opportunity to serve China's domestic payments market — Visa because it's a gigantic market and China because it wanted to maintain the fiction it was open.

Visa has had a toehold in the People's Republic of China since 1987 when the state-owned Bank of China joined the global bank card association. However, in the subsequent four decades there hasn't been a single domestic Visa transaction in mainland China. Visa's Sino-opportunity has been limited to transactions with one leg outside China: Chinese paying for goods and services abroad, and foreigners paying for goods and services in or sending money to China. Chinese, however, can't use Visa to pay Chinese merchants.

In 2001, as part of its accession to the WTO, the PRC committed to completely open its domestic payments market by 2006. This was under paramount leader and, in the China context, relative liberalizer Jiang Zemin who continued Deng Xiaoping's strategy of "Hide your strength, bide your time," while strengthening China by economic reform and opening up to the world. When Beijing made its WTO commitment, the Middle Kingdom's current payments colossi didn't yet exist. Card network China UnionPay, or CUP, and mobile payments phenoms Alipay and WeChat Pay were launched in 2002, 2009, and 2013, respectively.

By 2006, no foreign network had processed a payment in mainland China.

In 2010, in the face of the PRC's flagrantly flouting its commitment, the U.S. filed a WTO complaint. In 2012, the U.S. substantially prevailed and Beijing said that it wouldn't appeal.

Beijing slow-walked the rollout of the application process for foreign payment networks.

In 2013, Beijing declared it was implementing its commitment.

In October 2014, China's State Council made an announcement signaling that foreign firms like Visa could apply to p rocess domestic bank card transactions. It formalized the decree in April 2015, providing separate stages for preparatory and operational license applications. In June 2016, the PBOC and the China Banking Regulatory Commission detailed ownership structure, security, local data-storage, and clearing standards requirements.

On June 30, 2017, the PBOC opened its formal application process. The following month Visa applied. True to form, the central bank dragged out the review process.

Read more:

  • How Canada's real-time payment rail challenges bank innovation
  • Fintechs asking for, and receiving, bank charters in 2026
  • Affirm's direct pitch to bank customers moves forward
  • Chime puts out the welcome mat for external AI agents

American Express formed a 50-50 joint venture with Chinese fintech LianLian Group, aligning with Beijing's preference for local partners. It applied later in 2017. Amex's joint venture was ultimately granted preparatory approval in November 2018 and a final operating license in June 2020. It started clearing domestic payments later in 2020. In a two-step process from December 2024 to June 2025, Amex took control of the joint venture, diluting LianLian down to 17.65%.

Mastercard considered applying both as a wholly foreign-owned enterprise and with local partners. In March 2019, it established a joint venture with NetsUnion Clearing Corporation — a clearing entity controlled by the central bank and Chinese state-owned banks — and submitted a formal application. The PBOC approved its preparatory application in February 2020 and granted final operational approval in November 2023. Mastercard processed its first domestic Chinese transaction in 2024.

Nevertheless, American Express and Mastercard remain largely irrelevant in China's enormous domestic market.

The path for the world's largest card network has been more difficult.

Visa's initial preparatory application in July 2017 was as a wholly owned subsidiary — Visa Information Technology (China) Co., Ltd. For three years, the PBOC declined to formally acknowledge the application. In May 2020, following the U.S.-China Phase One Economic and Trade Agreement, the PBOC at long last formally logged Visa's resubmitted application, yet left it in limbo for another six years.

After its nine-year pocket veto, the PBOC's October 2026 limited green light for Visa is intended as a public gesture as part of the PRC's ongoing trade negotiations with the Trump administration. Even if Beijing made it in good faith and intended to let Visa compete on a level playing field — a premise that strains credulity given the last quarter of a century — the world's leading card network would start at an immense competitive disadvantage. The Middle Kingdom's three domestic payments giants have enormous network mass, work well, and are habit for consumers and merchants.

In 2024, the 9.9 billion CUP cards issued by Chinese banks were nearly universally accepted across the country. In 2026, Alipay and WeChat Pay each had more than 900 million active monthly users and enjoyed near ubiquitous acceptance online and at the physical point of sale. In contrast, Visa's acceptance in China is paltry, principally serving international travelers and e-merchants selling abroad. Moreover, China's largest card issuers are state-owned banks. Notionally private-sector banks too must be mindful of Beijing's preferences, which decidedly don't include seeing an American payments giant scale in China.

Compared with 2001, China's economy and military budget are roughly 13 times larger today. Under Xi Jinping's increasingly centralized and nationalistic leadership, China is no longer hiding its strength and biding its time. It's flexing its might and is an open foe of America.

The PRC's 25-year stall has made a mockery of its WTO commitment. Washington and Visa have no reason to take its latest gesture seriously. Beijing is not going to permit U.S. payment networks to play a critical role in its domestic payment system.

data.title: Ransomware crew claims 5 banks and a CU; 2 confirm breaches
data.description:
• What's at stake: Storm has listed five U.S. banks holding about $6.1 billion in assets, plus Insight Credit Union, and four of the banks have not publicly confirmed or denied an incident.
  • Supporting data: Sawyer, a $285 million bank, notified 16,069 people that their names and Social Security numbers were taken, according to the Indiana attorney general's breach report.

Overview bullets generated by AI with editorial review.

Attackers stole files holding the names and Social Security numbers of 16,069 people from a New York community bank this summer, and the ransomware group that claimed the attack has named five other U.S. financial institutions as victims in a recent wave of attacks.

Sawyer Savings Bank in Saugerties, New York, closed all of its branches for a week in August. Days into the closure, a group calling itself Storm listed Sawyer on its leak site, where the gang names organizations it says it hit as a way of pressuring them to pay a ransom.

One of the other institutions Storm listed, Insight Credit Union in Winter Springs, Florida, reported a data breach to the Texas and Vermont attorneys general in notices dated Friday.

Storm has also claimed it hit Pioneer Bank in Albany, New York; The Cecilian Bank in Cecilia, Kentucky; First Secure Bank Group in Illinois; and The Poca Valley Bank in Walton, West Virginia.

A listing on a leak site is a claim, and gangs sometimes overstate what they took or whom they hit.

None of the four unconfirmed banks appears in the searchable breach records that six states publish: Texas, Vermont, California, Washington, Indiana or Massachusetts.

None of the six financial institutions responded to requests for comment. Constangy, Brooks, Smith & Prophete, the law firm that filed the notice for Sawyer, also did not respond to a request for comment.

The five banks and one credit union collectively hold about $6.7 billion in assets, according to call reports published by the Federal Deposit Insurance Corp. and National Credit Union Administration.

The breach at Sawyer took place at a vendor the bank relied on rather than the bank itself. Sawyer's New Hampshire filing said the incident happened inside the systems of its managed service provider, the outside firm that runs its IT.

Storm's leak site appears to belong to a group Microsoft tracks as Storm-1175, which Microsoft has said is likely exploiting a flaw in software those providers use to manage their clients' computers.

What Sawyer's filings say

Sawyer Savings Bank "identified a network disruption resulting from a security incident within the environment of its managed service provider" on Aug. 3, according to the Oct. 9 notice the bank's lawyers filed with the New Hampshire attorney general.

The bank's investigation found that "certain files were acquired by an unauthorized individual," according to the notice. Sawyer finished reviewing those files on Sept. 21 and mailed letters to the affected people on Oct. 9.

The files held names and Social Security numbers, according to the New Hampshire notice.

There is "NO evidence that debit card numbers, financial account numbers," or information in the bank's core banking system (the software that keeps its account records) "were involved," according to the letter to affected people attached to the New Hampshire notice.

Sawyer's breach affected 16,069 people in total, according to the list of breaches reported to Indiana's attorney general, published by the state.

None of the filings name the IT provider or say whether the attack involved ransomware, although Microsoft has said Storm-1175 deploys ransomware.

"We believe this was the result of a vendor vulnerability," James P. Whitaker, the bank's president and CEO, said in an Aug. 6 update to customers while its branches were closed.

Storm's list

Storm listed Sawyer on Aug. 7, according to an American Banker review of the listing at the time. It listed Pioneer the same day, then Cecilian on Aug. 23, Insight on Sept. 15 and Poca Valley on Sept. 30, according to ransomware.live, a site that tracks ransomware gangs' leak sites.

Storm listed First Secure Bank Group four times between Sept. 18 and Sept. 27, although it appears these separate listings each concern the same incident; one names the bank group, and the three others name each of the group's three banks.

Pioneer's parent company, Pioneer Bancorp, has filed no report of a cybersecurity incident with the Securities and Exchange Commission.

Insight's breach involved Social Security numbers, driver's license and other government ID numbers, and financial account and card numbers, according to the breach reports the Texas and Vermont attorneys general published.

Neither report about Insight gave a cause, a date for the incident or a total number of affected individuals.

The vendor link

Storm-1175 began deploying a new strain of ransomware called StormEncryptor on Aug. 2, according to an Aug. 7 post by Microsoft Threat Intelligence.

The group is "likely exploiting" a flaw in N-central, software from the vendor N-able that IT providers use to monitor and manage their clients' systems, the post said. Microsoft "has not confirmed" that, according to the post.

The N-central flaw became public Aug. 2, the same day N-able released a fix and urged all customers to upgrade "ASAP," according to the company's status page.

Storm's leak site posted its first victims on Aug. 7, and ransomware.live estimates the earliest of those attacks happened Aug. 3. Sawyer identified the incident inside its IT provider's system on Aug. 3.

The leak site's name and timing tie it to Storm-1175, but Microsoft's post does not mention the site, and Sawyer's filings do not name N-central.

N-able took the hosted version of N-central offline worldwide Monday, after a security researcher published code he said exploits more than 30 previously unknown flaws in the software, BleepingComputer reported. Those are different flaws from the one Microsoft linked to Storm-1175, which N-able fixed in August.

N-able told customers running N-central on their own servers to shut them down until it releases a fix, according to its status page.

"At this time, we have no evidence that any customer environment has been successfully exploited," N-able said on the page Tuesday about the latest round of flaws.

data.title: FTC emerges as main consumer-protection watchdog in D.C.
data.description:
• Key insight: The Federal Trade Commission has positioned itself as the main watchdog of nonbanks, stepping up oversight and enforcement amid a retreat by the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau.
  • What's at stake: The FTC is pursuing an anti-fraud mandate reining in scams, fraud and market distortions.

Though consumer protection at the federal level has ground to a halt under the second Trump administration, one agency is a notable exception: the Federal Trade Commission.

The FTC has maintained an active docket with aggressive oversight of major technology platforms and digital payment processors engaged in facilitating fraud and deceptive practices, including surveillance pricing and undisclosed fees.  In light of that record, financial services companies shouldn't assume that consumer-protection enforcement in Washington will be nonexistent for the next two years.

In the past six weeks alone, the FTC has filed 10 significant enforcement actions, including a $225 million settlement with the multilevel marketer Amway and a $100 million settlement with Corplay, for charging unauthorized, hidden fees to fuel-card customers. In just two years, the FTC has brought in nearly $3 billion in restitution to consumers. 

The shift has less to do with any specific policy goals of the Trump administration and more to do with the agency's personnel. FTC Director Andrew Ferguson and Christopher Mufarrige, director of the FTC's Bureau of Consumer Protection, have worked to bring more enforcement actions over the past two years. 

"If you were to talk to Director Mufarrige, he would say the FTC is a law-enforcement agency focused on identifying fraud and the traditional unfair and deceptive practices that disrupt the competitive process," said Bradford Hardin, a partner at the law firm Davis Wright Tremaine. 

On Monday, the White ​House nominated ​Mufarrige to be the third Republican ⁠commissioner on the FTC's five-member board, which ⁠requires Senate approval. 

Mufarrige and his No. 2 Levi Swank, the deputy director of litigation at the FTC's bureau of consumer protection, have an anti-fraud enforcement agenda. In addition to deceptive billing practices, the FTC is focused on threats from AI-accelerated cyber fraud and financial losses from customer cyber scams. In the past two years, the FTC has brought in nearly $3 billion, outpacing the Biden administration's more than $2 billion of redress over four years. 

The FTC's authority is generally limited to nonbanks, including payment processors and auto dealers, but it also shares certain powers with the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau.

For example, the FTC regulates the privacy and security of consumer information, the collection and use of consumer credit information, and also enforces against nonbanks the Truth in Lending Act, the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act and the Electronic Fund Transfer Act. It can also enforce the federal prohibition on unfair and deceptive practices against nonbanks.

Apart from the FTC, enforcement of consumer-protection laws has collapsed to near-zero at the federal level. Federal enforcement declined throughout 2025, in line with the Trump administration's policy goals to reduce the footprint of the CFPB and prudential regulators, resulting in "minimal actions and penalties compared to prior years," according to research from global consulting firm BRG.

The sharp decline of federal enforcement actions by the Federal Reserve, Federal Deposit Insurance Corp. and the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, along with the CFPB,  stands in contrast to a pattern of steady enforcement by state attorneys general.

"Enforcement is simply not a priority for this administration," said Hardin. 

With the CFPB on ice, the FTC has emerged as the Trump administration's primary watchdog, albeit focused on an aggressive anti-fraud mandate and a belief in free-market competition. 

The FTC recently expanded a landmark $2.5 billion settlement with Amazon over deceptive sign-ups and hidden cancellation hurdles of Amazon Prime. It also has slapped industry giants, including Walmart, Uber, DoorDash and Target, with inquiries on how consumer data and AI algorithms dictate dynamic pricing and worker pay.

The FTC currently has just two commissioners after President Trump fired two Democratic commissioners, Rebecca Slaughter and Alvaro Bedoya, in March 2025. Trump claimed the president can fire members of independent commissions — at any time and without cause — and the Supreme Court agreed with him. In June, the court overturned precedent that insulated federal regulators such as the FTC from direct White House control over policy, though it carved out an exception for the Federal Reserve.

Joe Simonson, a White House senior policy advisor who serves as an FTC spokesman, said  there is no statutory language dictating when FTC members should be nominated and confirmed. 

"The president, the White House, has not nominated Democratic commissioners, and that's his prerogative, and the Supreme Court has upheld that prerogative," Simonson told American Banker.

Read more:

  • OCC: Banks need strong controls when delegating to AI agents
  • Democratic wave gives state AGs more enforcement sway
  • Midterm drubbing may complicate GOP lame duck priorities
  • FDIC taking more piecemeal approach to bank failures

While the CFPB has not completely vanished — the agency is quietly conducting bank examinations, rolling back policies implemented during Democratic administrations and keeping a handful of enforcement investigations alive — its posture is a shadow of its former self. 

Staff morale at the CFPB has hit rock-bottom, and public enforcement actions have plummeted. Some enforcement attorneys are being moved into regulations and rule-writing roles as the bureau waits for Brian Johnson, the former No. 2 at the agency in the first Trump administration, to be confirmed by the Senate during the lame-duck session. 

"The problem with the approach they've taken so far is they've just been cutting staff," said Konrad Alt, a co-founder and managing partner at Klaros Group, an advisory and investment firm. "If there's another crisis, which there will be, they've got no old approach, and they've got no new approach, either."

data.title: BofA has 5 million wealthy customers outside Merrill. Can it win their assets?
data.description:
• Key insight: Like many wealth managers, Bank of America gauges its success largely on its ability to bring in new client assets. In an ambitious plan, its CEO is setting his sights on doubling those NNA inflows in the next few years.
  • Expert quote: "We've had one of our best recruiting years ever, recruiting experienced [financial advisors] and our attrition is at sort of a decade low. So we're doing really well there and building and retaining and growing our financial advisor force." — Bank of America CEO Brian Moynihan

A year after setting a goal of bringing in as much as $150 billion in new fee-generating client assets a year, the head of Bank of America is acknowledging "we've got our work to do."
Speaking last week at the BancAnalysts Association of Boston Conference, Bank of America CEO Brian Moynihan said his firm has brought in roughly $65 billion in new assets this year into fee-generating accounts at Merrill and its other wealth management businesses and is on track for $80 billion by the end of the year. Getting to the $135 billion to $150 billion by 2028 to 2030, a goal Merrill executives talked about at an investor's day presentation a year ago, will require the firm to "double those [numbers] from where we are today," Moynihan said.

"Obviously, we've got our work to do here," Moynihan said.  

READ MORE: Merrill announces laser-targeted advisor bonus incentives for 2027 

BofA has a lot of ground to gain with at least one Wall Street rival

As AI and other technology enable advisors to serve more clients, wealth managers have come to gauge their success less by their advisor headcounts and more on their asset totals. With $5.1 trillion in client assets — including investments, deposits and loans — Merrill and Bank of America's private bank are easily among the biggest firms in the industry.

Yet their asset gathering ability lags behind at least one key rival. Morgan Stanley, with just over $8.4 trillion under management, brought in $280 billion in net new assets in the third quarter alone, much of it coming from employees of private firms selling stock in initial public offerings.

To boost its asset inflows, Moynihan said Bank of America is seeking to add to its advisor headcount with a training program with roughly 2,500 enrollees and a new emphasis on recruiting from rivals.

"We've had one of our best recruiting years ever recruiting experienced [financial advisors], and our attrition is at sort of a decade low," he said. "So we're doing really well there and building and retaining and growing our financial advisor force."

Louis Diamond, the CEO of the recruiting firm Diamond Consultants, said Merrill's advisor losses do indeed seem to be back to normal levels and "not as elevated as they were a couple of years ago." Diamond also credited Merrill for some significant recruiting wins. They include an advisor duo that had been managing $1.2 billion for UBS in Santa Fe, New Mexico; and a four-person team previously managing $1.5 billion at Morgan Stanley in Boulder, Colorado.

Like many wealth managers, one of Merrill's biggest difficulties is the sheer array of choices advisors now have when they're seeking to change firms. It's not only competing against wirehouses like Wells Fargo, which is seeing its own recruiting resurgence, but also any number of independent broker-dealers and RIAs offering a greater degree of independence along with often quite-generous transition deals.

"There's a lot of good with Merrill that advisors appreciate," Diamond said. "If someone really prioritizes lending and a firm with a great reputation, they certainly could be it. But there's also a number of other firms that can check that box, too."

READ MORE: Why a $1.5B wirehouse team considered independence but jumped to Merrill 

Merrill, BofA private bank mine firm's other business for assets

Bank of America is also looking to bolster its wealth management units with assets brought in from its other lines of business. Moynihan estimated Bank of America has 5 million high net worth customers of its retail and other banks who don't also use the firm's wealth services. The same is true, he said, for roughly 1 million clients whose workplace benefits are administered by the firm.

So far this year, Moynihan said, 130,000 customers have been referred to the wealth management unit either from other businesses at the firm or those businesses from wealth management. Roughly 45% of the private bank's new clients have come from these introductions, he said.

"All we have to do is keep referring those clients into the private bank, into Merrill Lynch, and we will grow our assets overall," Moynihan said.

Dean Athanasia, Bank of America co-president, said that if Bank of America brought in just 1.5% to 2% of its high net worth clients' assets into its wealth business, it would add $100 billion.  

"It's a big number … but referrals are up 25% year over year," Athanasia said. "So when we're looking at where we're going, we're progressing, more clients are coming in, more referrals coming in, but those assets are coming in with them."

READ MORE: Bank of America gives Merrill Lynch an AI makeover 

Higher margins, lending balances and alts investments

Meanwhile, Moynihan noted progress toward another goal for the firm's Global Wealth & Investment Management business: attaining a pretax margin of 30% in the 2028-to-2030 timeframe. This margin — the percentage of revenue left over after expenses other than taxes — now stands at roughly 28%.

Moynihan called wealth management "our least efficient business." Even so, net income for Global Wealth & Investment Management has risen by 31% year over year so far in 2026 to hit $4 billion.

In other signs of progress, Moynihan said 25,000 wealth professionals at the firm are now using AI to automate routine tasks and are, as a result, "spending more time with clients, accessing more clients, building those relationships, doing more with them."

He noted that the total for loans arranged through Bank of America's wealth management business have risen by 12% year over year to $283 billion, although 42% of Merrill clients still don't hold bank deposits with the firm. Many wealth managers view banking products and services as a particularly good way to make wealth management clients "sticky," or unlikely to move their assets to a rival firm.

Moynihan also said Bank of America's wealth units saw a steep increase in helping clients move money into private equity, private credit and other alternative assets. He said such flows have increased by 16% year over year so far in 2026 — without providing a total number — and the firm estimates private bank customers could eventually hold $260 billion in alternatives.

data.title: Fed's Bowman says 'there is still work to do' on inflation
data.description:
• Key insight: The Federal Reserve vice chair for supervision stopped just short of endorsing a rate hike in December, but noted that price pressures are broadening beyond imports, energy and data center components.
  • Expert quote: "Today, I am seeing signs that inflation pressures are persisting, while labor market conditions appear to be firming. This indicates that there is still work to do to bring inflation closer to 2%." — Fed Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle Bowman

Federal Reserve Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle Bowman said the central bank has more work to do to bring down inflation, but stopped short of explicitly endorsing a December rate hike.

In a speech at an event hosted by the Council on Foreign Relations on Tuesday, Bowman said inflation has been "more persistent" than she anticipated and has "shown recent signs of broadening." She also noted that tighter monetary policy could prove ineffective in stifling price growth in this environment and could weaken the parts of the economy that are already under stress. 

Bowman said she wants to see more data about how the economy develops and responds to the Federal Open Market Committee's 25 basis point increase to the federal funds rate in September.

"Today, I am seeing signs that inflation pressures are persisting, while labor market conditions appear to be firming. This indicates that there is still work to do to bring inflation closer to 2%," she said. "Given the recent market volatility, I will also continue to closely monitor how developments in financial conditions influence the economic outlook."

Bowman's remarks came hours after the Bureau of Labor Statistics released its consumer price index inflation report for October. The report showed prices grew 0.4% last month, surpassing the consensus forecast and continuing a troubling upward trend in inflation. 

In her remarks, Bowman divided the contributing factors behind this price growth into four categories: high energy costs, tariffs, artificial intelligence-related price pressures and "persistent effects from the inflationary shocks in recent years." While she anticipates the first three categories abating, she said the lingering question is whether broader price growth will follow suit or continue to expand.

"It is important to ensure that those inflationary pressures do not intensify, further broaden, or become embedded in consumer and business expectations," she said. "But today's consumer price index data suggest that inflation pressures may persist for longer."

While Bowman stopped short of calling for a rate hike next month, she said that her "focus" has shifted from the employment side of the Fed's dual mandate to the price stability side — a notable shift for Bowman, who has been among the FOMC's most public skeptic of the wisdom of further rate hikes in recent months. 

Bowman's comments come as two other FOMC voters endorsed increasing their benchmark interest rate by at least a quarter percentage point at their meeting next month. 

Fed Gov. Christopher Waller, who delivered a speech in London on Tuesday morning before the CPI report was released, signaled a willingness to support a half-percentage point increase if month-over-month inflation rose by more than 0.3%. 

"Hiking only 25 basis points would put our credibility at risk, a risk I am not eager to take," Waller said.

Read more:

  • OCC: Banks need strong controls when delegating to AI agents
  • Democratic wave gives state AGs more enforcement sway
  • Midterm drubbing may complicate GOP lame duck priorities
  • FDIC taking more piecemeal approach to bank failures

In a speech of her own on Tuesday, Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas President Lorie Logan said she believes the current federal funds rate, set at a target range of 3.75% to 4%, translates to a real — meaning inflation-adjusted — interest rate of around 0.78%, below what she believes to be the neutral rate of interest, which she pegs between 1% and 1.85%. 

Logan said she believes the Fed should tighten its policy rate by 50 basis points to make it restrictive enough to begin curbing inflation. She said the FOMC does not need to make that adjustment all in one shot at its next meeting, but argued that it must start moving in that direction.

"It remains clear to me, given the current outlook, that the FOMC needs to implement at least two more 25-basis-point rate increases," she said. "The exact pace of increases could depend on the near-term economic and financial environment. It may be possible to move more rapidly this winter than the FOMC has moved so far this fall."

Bowman does not seem to share the sense of urgency expressed by Logan and Waller, noting repeatedly that she wants to give the situation time and assess the data on market developments before adjusting policy. 

Instead, Bowman is weighing the potential costs of increasing interest rates at a time when private interest rates are already on the rise and equity prices are trending down. She said these forces could serve as a natural corrective to an overexuberant market and suggested that further action by the Fed could cause major disruptions in the economy.
