"Lower equity prices could undermine the resilience in consumer spending and higher interest rates could further strain interest-rate-sensitive sectors of the economy, like housing and small business investment," she said. "I will continue to closely monitor developments in credit and equity markets to assess risks to economic growth and financial stability."

Bowman also noted that disruptions to the AI sector could reverberate back to the banking system. While the biggest lenders to data center developers and AI firms — including banks as well as life insurance companies, mutual funds, pension funds and private credit firms — appear well positioned to absorb potential losses, she said it is difficult to map out the risks in this part of the economy precisely.

"Most of these entities are well capitalized and have stable funding," she said. "But the complex nature of the financing structures makes it difficult to properly assess counterparty risk."

data.title: Card balances rise, but pace of growth slows: New York Fed
data.description:
• Key insight: The New York Fed's latest quarterly report on household debt and credit reveals an uptick in credit-card balances. But the rate at which those balances are increasing has slowed.
  • Expert quote: "Balances only fall when something weird happens." — Ted Rossman, analyst at Money Management International

U.S. credit-card balances climbed to new heights in the third quarter, part of a broader increase in household debt across loan categories, the Federal Reserve Bank of New York said Tuesday. 

But the pace of growth has eased from recent years, and delinquency rates, while still higher than they were during and immediately following the pandemic, appear to be stabilizing. 

Card balances rose 4.2% year over year to $1.29 trillion, the highest level recorded by the regional Fed bank, according to its quarterly analysis of household debt and credit. Meanwhile, the percentage of borrowers who were 90 days or more late on their card payments remained in the 12% range, where it has hovered for most of the past seven quarters.

The uptick in card balances may reflect a steady, growing economy, said Ted Rossman, an analyst at Money Management International who reviewed the New York Fed's data. Even as consumer sentiment about inflation and affordability remain largely negative, Americans are still spending money, as several banks reported during their third-quarter earnings calls.

"If credit-card balances were falling, that would probably say something negative about the economy," Rossman told American Banker. "Balances only fall when something weird happens."

If balances keep ticking up by around 4% or so, that could be viewed positively, Rossman added. Moreover, the numbers don't reflect consumers who pay off their balances in full every month, he said.

"Those numbers I actually think are Goldilocks numbers — not too hot, not too cold," he said. "I feel like that would be sustainable."

Credit-card debt has climbed by 61% over the past five years, as balances rose in the years following the pandemic. It exceeded $1 trillion for the time ever in the second quarter of 2023.

At that time, the 90-day delinquency rate was 8%. As of the most recent quarter, it was 12.90%, up from 12.41% recorded in the same quarter last year, but down slightly from 12.92% in the second quarter of 2026. 

Credit-card borrowers' transition into early delinquencies and serious delinquencies in the third quarter "improved slightly," the New York Fed said Tuesday in a press release. In a related blog post that analyzed credit-card debt by income level, the New York Fed said the delinquency gap between borrowers living in higher-income areas and those living in lower-income ones has expanded, with lower-income borrowing bearing more stress.

Notably, delinquency rates for cards issued during the pandemic are easing, the New York Fed said. If those rates keep abating, "the elevated delinquencies of the past few years may prove to be more of a pandemic-era echo than a permanent feature of the credit card market, one that may continue to fade as 2020-22 [card] vintages" shrink.

Read more:

  • OCC: Banks need strong controls when delegating to AI agents
  • Democratic wave gives state AGs more enforcement sway
  • Midterm drubbing may complicate GOP lame duck priorities
  • FDIC taking more piecemeal approach to bank failures

Along with credit-card balances, debts for mortgages, auto loans and home equity lines of credit also picked up during the quarter, the New York Fed said. In total, debt expanded by $334 billion, or about 1.8% in the third quarter, to $19.1 trillion. About half of the increase in mortgage debt was tied to a re-reporting of balances after a reporting gap in the previous quarter, the report said.

The New York Fed's latest data was released the same day that the October consumer price index numbers were unveiled. According to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, inflation last month rose 0.4% from September, putting more pressure on the Federal Reserve to hike rates.

data.title: As bank BNPL grows, consumers could face added risk
data.description:
• Key insight: Bank-led BNPL is expanding, according to Equipifi's index of its users. 
  • Forward look: As BNPL grows, banks will face different risks, including consumers' cash management.

With the trend toward buy now/pay later lending growing, banks that offer the payment option are facing a growing and different type of risk.
There will be $21.3 billion in BNPL e-commerce holiday sales in the U.S. in 2026, according to Adobe Digital Insights, up 6.6% from 2025 and about 8% of the total $275.1 billion online holiday sales expected for 2026. Bank BNPL processor Equipifi says the amount of BNPL that's coming through the bank channel is on the rise.

"This is an opportunity for banks but with a major caveat," Stewart Watterson, a strategic advisor for Datos Insights, told American Banker. "It's a new layer of consumer cash flow management risk and there's not a lot of data out on it yet."

BNPL at the bank

Equipifi, which tracks BNPL programs at the banks and credit unions in its network, says weekly BNPL volume in the holiday shopping season is expected to be double the average over 2025, with the number of consumers using bank/credit union BNPL expected to rise 60%. Equipifi did not release financial numbers, but said its index covers more than one billion transactions at more than 100 financial institutions and 4 million households over the past 12 months. 

The number that jumps out is the 60% rise in people using BNPL through their own bank or credit union, Phil Philliou, a payments consultant, told American Banker. "The fintechs have owned this at checkout. Now the bank and credit union is showing up inside its own app and saying 'you can split that into four,' which is a much easier sell than signing up with someone new," Philliou said.

Equipifi, which debuted its white-label BNPL service in 2023, has expanded its current bank and credit union network to about 150, according to Bryce Deeney, Equipfi's co-founder and CEO.

"For institutions that didn't have their own BNPL program, their customers could only get it from third parties," Deeney told American Banker.

Non-banks such as Klarna (which is a bank in Sweden), PayPal and Afterpay have traditionally dominated BNPL, banks are slowly embracing BNPL as a way to control more of their consumer's business while adding an option for merchants. Citigroup, for example, offers Citi Pay installments as a means to combine its merchant and consumer businesses–and has reported double digital monthly growth in the product's first year. 

U.S. Bank recently launched the Split Card, which converts eligible purchases into fixed-term installments, specifically to appeal to younger consumers who prefer pay-over-time products to traditional revolving cards.

"The interesting shift for banks is that BNPL is no longer solely a checkout proposition," 

Alyson Clarke, principal analyst at Forrester Research, told American Banker, adding major issuers already let eligible customers make a purchase and then convert qualifying card transactions into installment plans afterward. "That could be particularly relevant during the holidays because consumers can look across several purchases after the fact and decide which larger expenses they want to spread out."

For smaller banks and credit unions, partners such as Equipifi, FIS, Fiserv, Splitit have emerged as options. 

"We think there's a lot of consumers that are using BNPL for the first time. They never used it from a third party but will use it from an institution that they trust," Deeney said. 

What could go wrong?

As BNPL has grown globally, so has the concern that it creates credit risk for the consumers and merchants. 

Regulators and bank executives sounded alarms about unclear repayment terms, limited credit-bureau reporting, third-party compliance risks, and borrowers accumulating multiple BNPL loans. About 86% of surveyed executives at banks offering BNPL said the products create some degree of credit risk, according to American Banker research. Real disposable income per capita grew just 0.7% year over year in Q2, while the personal savings rate fell from 6.9% in Q1 2024 to 4.4% in Q2 2026, according to Forrester Research.

At the same time, 23% of U.S. online adults say they have less money available for the holidays than last year, even though 38% expect to spend about the same, Forrester reports.

The difference in risk depends on the type of consumer. Consumers with an existing credit card have an existing profile and pose less risk, according to Watterson.

"With banks, they have already lent the consumers money if the consumer has credit," Watterson said. "If the consumer wants to restructure that it's fine as long as they are managing their cash flow well." 

On the debit or cash side, it's a different risk for banks because of the nature of a BNPL transaction, which transforms a cash purchase into a credit transaction, according to Watterson. "This complicates the cash flow process," he said. Equipifi recently launched risk-based pricing for BNPL. That enables lenders to tailor BNPL terms to each consumer's real-time financial context while managing competitive pressure from BNPL fintechs, according to Deeney. 

Deeney said that an account holder who has banked with their institution for more than 10 years with a high cash balance can have easier access to a BNPL loan. At the same time, if there's "signals" in their account history that reveal an elevated risk, risk-based pricing can enable that loan to be approved but at a higher rate. 

Read more:

  • Bankers swing to negative view on funding costs: Survey
  • How agentic commerce is changing the customer experience
  • Why the FTC and 8 states are suing payments fintech Toast
  • $6B Binance heist provokes stablecoin freeze dilemma

"The biggest improvement is making BNPL underwriting relational and real-time. Banks and credit unions already own the data that speaks most directly to BNPL risk: deposit, payment and overdraft history," Deeney said, noting that BNPL is small-dollar installment lending, typically repaid over a few months. "Leaning on traditional credit scores doesn't answer what an account holder can afford to repay right now. This is something cash flow underwriting addresses, especially if lending decisions incorporate tenure, direct deposit relationship, and repayment history."
Banks and credit unions may have an edge, according to Philliou. 

"They already see the paycheck coming in and the bills going out, so they can make a better call on who can handle an installment plan than a lender who only sees one purchase," he said. "That should mean fewer people getting in over their heads, if the banks actually use that data and act on it."

data.title: RIA Leaders: Top 10 firms by number of financial advisors for 2026
data.description:
Even though the largest fee-only registered investment advisory firms collectively manage almost $4 trillion in client assets, nearly every one of them is technically a small business.

Just four fee-only RIAs out of more than 5,500 that fit Financial Planning's criteria for the RIA Leaders ranking, based on an analysis of Securities and Exchange Commission filings by data partner FINTRX, have more than 500 employees. One of the most commonly cited components of the U.S. Small Business Administration's definition of "small business" applies that moniker to companies that have no more than 500 staff members. 

But the 10 firms ranked below by the number of financial advisors stand out from fee-only peers for their substantial bases of talent in a field with a well-documented recruiting and retention problem.

The top three firms in the group — St. Louis-based Moneta Group Investment Advisors, Torrance, California-based EP Wealth Advisors and Rockford, Illinois-based Savant Wealth Management — were the same as last year, although EP Wealth and Moneta Group switched places in the No. 2 and No. 3 spots from 2025. 

As one of the industry's most active RIA M&A firms, Savant has now topped the list three years in a row. With wealth management firms waging a constant struggle to recruit and retain top advisor talent, the companies that reward them through effective compensation plans and operational aid reap big advantages.

"If you don't have the right ingredients, the value propositions for the advisors, then there's no reason for them to come to you," said Ritik Malhotra, the founder and CEO of New York-based RIA services firm Savvy Wealth. "They're extremely sharp, they're extremely discerning about, what is the platform going to do for me? And that's how they're making their decisions about, where am I going to affiliate?"

Scroll down the slideshow to see which fee-only RIAs that provide planning services to clients have the most financial advisors. For last year's rankings, click here.

And see other RIA Leaders 2026 coverage:

  • The custody fee conundrum
  • The top 20 fee-only RIAs ranked by AUM in 2026
  • Download FP's list of the 150 largest fee-only RIAs

Notes: FP's data provider for the RIA Leaders feature, FINTRX, produced the ranking by applying the following six criteria to firms' required SEC Form ADV filings in August:

  • Firms must have zero registered representatives of a broker-dealer.
  • At least 50% of the firm's clients must be individuals or high net worth individuals.
  • Firms must not list commissions as a compensation arrangement.
  • Firms must have more than zero financial planning clients.
  • Firms must not list commission-taking businesses in "other business activities."
  • Firms cannot be affiliated under common ownership with commission-taking businesses.

In the absence of an official regulatory classification and definition for the titles "financial planner" or "financial advisor," FP is citing the numbers available through FINTRX's analysis of how many "producing financial advisors" there are at each firm.

In the wake of the revelations involving Forbes and Shook Research (now called Veritant), it is important to state that no members of the teams at FP and FINTRX exchanged any money in the production of RIA Leaders, and no RIAs listed in the feature paid anything for their places in the rankings.

data.title: North Dakota bank looks to put down roots in Dallas
data.description:
Key takeaway: First International joins a lengthy list of banks that have recently moved to enter or expand in Dallas, a market that's attractive due to its population growth and concentration of wealth.

Supporting data: The North Texas city is home to an estimated 72,000 millionaires. 

First International Bank & Trust in Watford City, North Dakota, has become the latest bank to hear Dallas' siren song, striking a deal Tuesday to acquire a three-branch community bank headquartered inside the massive Texas metroplex. 

Both First International and the $650 million-asset seller, Dominion Bancshares, are privately held, so financial terms of the transaction, which is expected to close in the first quarter of 2027, were not disclosed. 

"This is a landmark moment for FIBT and one of the most exciting opportunities in our company's history,"  Peter Stenehjem, CEO of the family-owned, $6.2 billion-asset First International, said in a press release.

Dominion operates two branches in Dallas and one in the East Texas community of Grapeland where its bank subsidiary, Dominion Bank, was founded in 1911. Known as Grapeland State Bank for most of its history, the company rebranded and moved its headquarters to Dallas after an investor group led by Chairman and CEO Thomas Mastor acquired it in 2019. 

Dominion reported 46 employees on its June 30 call report. First International stated it expects to offer all of them positions in the merged institution. It tabbed Mastor to serve as its Texas president and to serve on First International's board. 

Mastor has deep roots in Dallas. Prior to launching Dominion, he co-founded Sovereign Bank there in 2004, building it into a $1 billion-asset institution before its sale to Veritex Holdings in 2017.

"FIBT's history, family ownership and long-term approach stood out to us," Mastor said in the press release. He added that Dominion's bankers "will have greater capacity to support customers' ambitions through larger lending opportunities, expanded financial solutions and enhanced capabilities, while maintaining … localized relationships and personalized service."

The population of the Dallas-Fort Worth metroplex reached approximately 8.5 million in 2025, an 11% increase from 2020, according to the U.S. Census Bureau. Dallas ranks among the wealthiest cities in the nation, with more than 72,000 millionaires, according to high-net-worth residency consultant Henley and Partners. 

The combination of increased population and growing wealth has proved attractive to both out-of-state and international banks. So far in 2026, the $43.8 billion-asset MidFirst Bank in Oklahoma City and the $1.1 trillion-asset Scotiabank in Toronto, have announced plans to acquire Dallas-based banks.

A number of other lenders — including the $130.7 billion-asset Pinnacle Financial Partners, the $51 billion-asset Associated Banc-Corp, and the $703 billion-asset U.S. Bancorp — have announced plans to establish or expand their Dallas commercial-banking teams.

Earlier this month, the $1.38 billion-asset SBIC Bank, a subsidiary of the State Bank of India, opened a branch in Frisco, a Dallas suburb. 

Read more:

  • Bankers swing to negative view on funding costs: Survey
  • How agentic commerce is changing the customer experience
  • Why the FTC and 8 states are suing payments fintech Toast
  • Key turns to acquisitions during middle-market M&A lull

Peter Stenehjem represents the fourth generation of his family to lead First International. The bank was founded in 1910 as Farmers State Bank in Arnegard, North Dakota, by brothers Odin and Gerhard Stenehjem.
The bank, which adopted the First International brand in 1934, expanded significantly under the leadership of Stephen Stenehjem, who served 34 years as CEO. During his tenure, First International moved into Minneapolis, South Dakota and Arizona, and it acquired the payments processor InterceptEFT, which it rebranded as Kotapay.

Stephen Stenehjem's son, Peter Stenehjem, succeeded him in 2025.

data.title: JPMorganChase to use OpenAI models for coding, security
data.description:
• Key insight: OpenAI announced it's signed a contract with JPMorganChase to use the frontier AI model provider's technology in software development and cybersecurity.
  • Expert quote: "JPMorganChase is increasingly setting the architectural and economic blueprint for how banks adopt AI."—Krish Subramanian, founder and managing partner at Rishidot Research

JPMorganChase signed a contract with OpenAI to use the tech company's Codex AI agents to write, review, debug and ship code, OpenAI President Greg Brockman announced via social media. The bank will also use OpenAI models for cybersecurity.

The announcement is significant because JPMorganChase rarely announces vendor agreements and what the largest U.S. bank does with technology, other banks tend to follow.

In the past, JPMorganChase has acknowledged the use of other AI models, for instance its LLM Suite that gives employees access to models including OpenAI's GPT-4 and Anthropic's Claude. Its engineering and internal analysis teams use Claude; its developers use Github Copilot among other AI coding models.

"JPMorganChase is increasingly setting the architectural and economic blueprint for how banks adopt AI," Krish Subramanian, founder and managing partner at Rishidot Research, told American Banker. "By treating AI as core infrastructure rather than an innovation expense, they're potentially establishing a new baseline for technology investment, operating models, and competitive expectations across banking."

The bank's scale and investment "could shape the technology architectures, infrastructure requirements, and vendor ecosystems that the rest of the industry adopts," he said.

A JPMorganChase spokeswoman said the bank uses a variety of tools, "which we have consistently said we will do. And we'll continue to use multiple." She declined to share terms of the contract or answer questions about which OpenAI models the bank is using besides Codex.

During the bank's third-quarter earnings call last month, Chief Financial Officer Jeremy Barnum said it's spending "something like $700 million annually" on AI. "If you sort of price out the amount of time we're all spending thinking about it, you can probably get a higher number, too. So at this point, it's not really something that you can ring fence. It's pretty well diffused inside the whole institution, and it's obviously like a very, very high priority."

The benefits of AI use didn't show up in the bank's quarterly results, he conceded.

"I think that's probably not that surprising because … it takes a long time to really do things that are visible at an institution of our size," Barnum said. Some experiments with using AI to rewrite "minor legacy tools" in a couple of weeks "didn't work perfectly, but you're starting to see some really exciting opportunities for acceleration and productivity change," he said. "So how long it's going to take for that to show up, we'll see. And obviously, some of those benefits are going to be offset with token costs, which is a whole other conversation, but we're excited."

Barnum also said the bank's strategy is focused on "minimizing lock-in and maximizing optionality and the ability to manage costs. So part of the strategy is model agnosticism, harness agnosticism and ability to run both proprietary models, but also open weight and open source models, some of which we run in our data center."

Bank regulators have not offered model risk guidance specific to generative and agentic AI, though the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency recently published a framework for examiners to make risk-based assessments of AI used in banks, the way they would any technology deployment.

The most noteworthy aspect of the OpenAI deal, according to Linas Beliunas, venture advisor at EQT Ventures, is JPMorganChase's use of OpenAI models for cybersecurity.

"Helping employees write documents is one thing, asking a vendor to help secure a bank means trusting it with a very different class of work," he said. "This is a much bigger ambition than giving staff a chatbot."

data.title: Banks top JD Power originator ranking as digital drives satisfaction
data.description:
• Key Insight: Uncover how traditional banks dominated JD Power's latest mortgage origination satisfaction rankings.
  • What's at Stake: Nonbank lenders fighting to retain market share against banks with pre-existing customer relationships.
    Overview bullets generated by AI with editorial review. 

For the second consecutive year, banks occupied the top slots on JD Power's Mortgage Origination Satisfaction Study, benefitting from the importance of digital experiences to borrowers.
The results reinforce findings in the Mortgage Servicer Digital Experience study released in October, where banks had the higher scores than the nonbanks graded.

A big part of the findings then was the banks had the advantage because of multiple product relationships.

This is the case in the originator survey as well, said Bruce Gehrke, senior director of wealth and lending intelligence at JD Power.

Customers looking for the trust factor

"Digital is such a big part of the experience now, but it's also relationship based," Gehrke said. This creates a trust component with the banks.

"I open up a checking and savings account or other accounts with a financial institution," he continued. "It takes a certain level of trust to do that, and it's not as big of a jump then to go for a loan as it would be to a completely unknown lender."

This comes out in the data JD Power has for younger borrowers. But across the board some respondents consider it riskier to go to someone new for a mortgage.

Originators that scored best in this year's survey

Chase was the top scorer this year, at 789; It is a gain of 18 points over last year's 771. It was the top scorer in the servicer satisfaction survey released in the summer.

Bank of America remained No. 2, but its score fell to 788 from 792. The bank rounding out the three was PNC, at 785, a significant jump from 721 one year ago, when it was third from the bottom.

Tied for fourth at 776 were nonbanks Movement Mortgage and Rocket. Movement's score was unchanged from last year, where it was the top scoring independent mortgage bankers.

Rocket's score increased from 762 one year ago.

Citi, the only originator with a score over 800 last year at 802, was at 766 this year.

This year's Originator Satisfaction survey returned an industry average of 760, equal to last year's findings. JD Power found improvements in digital channels and the ratings for lender staff were offset by declines in the level of trust established and opinions on keeping borrowers informed during the origination process.

What changed from the 2025 results

"I expected it to fall back a little, given the extra challenges we've seen this year, just financially certainly in the housing industry, and after such a large gain last year, where the majority of almost every lender was up and some really significantly," Gehrke said.

The survey noted some of the friction is coming out of the process.

For example, documents are now being sent directly to the lender from the source, rather than having to be emailed or copied.

The process improvement is likely a result of the lower volume, leaving lenders with more capacity to deal with such things.

"Some of the satisfaction indexes that we see in this study are higher than any other financial study that we have out there right now," said Gehrke. "So of all things in this environment, the mortgage origination process is really delivering."

Furthermore, the business remains highly competitive and "competition drives improvement," he said.

Which areas still can improve

Still, a few negatives abound in the data.

In particular, Power found 58% of those taking this year's survey said they received a same-day response for their lender, down 4 percentage points from 2025.

While still at a relatively healthy 88%, the share who said they had a main point of contact for their mortgage fell from 91%.

A larger share of borrowers experienced a problem after their loan was approved or when they went to closing.But what might give banks an advantage over nonbanks is those who had other financial products with the lender they applied to are more likely to trust that entity. This was to the point where they considered them a trusted advisor.

When it comes to a digital experience, two-thirds of Gen Y and Gen Z mortgage borrowers preferred self-service tools for getting a loan; but almost half of the cohort added they wished their representative had been more involved.

Gehrke pointed to other studies which show Chime opening more new checking accounts than the traditional banks, showing younger generations aren't necessarily tied to a relationship with those institutions that older demographics are.

Yet the results also show that while they want better digital interactions, they also are looking for someone to be available to guide them if needed.

Power added these borrowers are also significantly more likely to shop around, to the point where they use artificial intelligence tools when researching mortgage providers. This raises the stakes for lenders to deliver on both expectations, it added.

In the overall business environment, banks have multiple business streams and this diversification puts them in a better position. But at the same time, Gehrke said they are not as willing to commit to residential real estate finance as much as an independent mortgage banker where it is the company's primary or only business line.

But, he reiterated, competition drives better experiences for everybody and the data shows it bumping down the negatives in the housing industry right now. 

How certain other lenders scored this year

Meanwhile, three lenders whose target market is veterans received scores but were not eligible to be ranked because they do not meet Power's criteria.

USAA scored 823 and Navy Federal was at 795, topping Chase, while Veterans United at 787 would have been behind B of A.

At the other end of the spectrum, Pennymac scored the lowest of the 17 originators listed this year, at 696; it was not ranked in 2025.

Freedom Mortgage, also not ranked last year, scored 706, while loanDepot received a 710 score, down from 722.

Mr. Cooper, last year's lowest scorer on the list of 25 originators at 697, was acquired by Rocket on Oct. 1, 2025. Truist received a 727 score, up from 709 for 2025.
